title: Kafka: durability and failure handling
seriesDescription: A Kafka deep dive for system design interviews: why Kafka exists, terminology, messages and keys, offsets and replication, when to use it, scalability, hot partitions, fault tolerance, retries, performance and retention.
description: Replication factor, acks, in-sync replicas, consumer failures, rebalancing and when to commit offsets.
source: Study notes: Kafka deep dive for system design interviews

questions.prompt: What does a replication factor of 3 mean?

options.text: Each partition has three copies: one leader and two followers on different brokers.
options.why: Right: one failure does not lose data.

options.text: The topic has three partitions in a typical production setup.
options.why: That is a partition count.

options.text: Messages are sent three times by the producer.
options.why: Replication is broker-side.

options.text: There are three producers per topic for most everyday workloads.
options.why: Unrelated; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: If one broker fails, the data is still on the other two.

options.text: A message is acknowledged only when all in-sync replicas have received it.
options.why: Right: the strongest durability guarantee.

options.text: The message is stored only on the leader before the reply.
options.why: That is weaker; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: The message is delivered to every consumer first.
options.why: Consumers are not involved.

options.text: The producer never retries under normal operating conditions.
options.why: Unrelated; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: Replication factor 3 plus acks=all: the message lives on several brokers before the producer hears done.

questions.prompt: An interviewer asks "what if Kafka goes down?" How can you respond?

options.text: Gently push back: Kafka is built to be always available, and a consumer failing is far more likely.
options.why: Right: design for the realistic failure.

options.text: Say Kafka never loses messages under any configuration for most everyday workloads under normal operating conditions.
options.why: Over-claiming; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Say you will not use Kafka at all as a general rule of thumb in the majority of deployments.
options.why: Avoids the question; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Refuse to discuss failures.
options.why: Not helpful; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: Kafka is always available, sometimes consistent.

questions.prompt: How does a restarted consumer know where to continue?

options.text: It resumes from its last committed offset.
options.why: Right: nothing is missed, a few messages may repeat.

options.text: It starts again from the very first message ever written.
options.why: Not the default; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: It reads only the newest message.
options.why: It would skip messages.

options.text: It asks the producer to resend everything.
options.why: Producers are not involved.

questions.explanation: Repeats are possible if it crashed before committing.

questions.prompt: A consumer in a group dies. What does Kafka do with its partitions?

options.text: It hands them to the remaining consumers, so every partition is still processed.
options.why: Right: rebalancing; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: It stops reading those partitions until the consumer returns without any extra configuration.
options.why: Work would stall; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: It deletes those partitions.
options.why: Data stays; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: It duplicates the partitions onto every consumer in a typical production setup.
options.why: Each is owned by one consumer.

questions.explanation: In a real group, Kafka decides which survivor gets which partition.

questions.prompt: A crawler commits the offset before storing the downloaded HTML, then crashes. What is the result?

options.text: Kafka thinks the page is done, so it is never crawled.
options.why: Right: committing too early loses work.

options.text: The page is crawled twice.
options.why: That happens if you commit after and crash.

options.text: Kafka re-downloads it automatically for most everyday workloads.
options.why: It will not know to; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Nothing; commits do not matter under normal operating conditions.
options.why: They decide what is skipped.

questions.explanation: Finish the work first, commit second, and keep each piece of work small.

questions.prompt: What is the cost of committing after the work is done and then crashing?

options.text: The message is read again and some work is repeated, but nothing is lost.
options.why: Right: at-least-once; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: The message is lost permanently without any extra configuration in a typical production setup.
options.why: That is the early-commit risk.

options.text: The topic is deleted.
options.why: Not real; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: The consumer group is disbanded forever as a general rule of thumb in the majority of deployments.
options.why: It rebalances; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: Keep per-message work small so less is repeated.

questions.prompt: True or false: only a follower that is fully in sync can be promoted to leader.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: an out-of-sync follower could lose messages.

options.text: False
options.why: Promoting an out-of-sync follower could lose data.

questions.explanation: That is why the in-sync replica set matters for durability.
